glossary.text: A licensed company that processes health insurance claims on the insurer's behalf, including cashless approvals at hospitals. The insurer remains accountable for what the TPA does, so its performance and controls are overseen here.

glossary.full: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
glossary.text: The regulator that licenses and supervises insurers, TPAs and intermediaries in India. Most obligations in the regulatory library come from its regulations and circulars.
The time taken to finish a step, such as deciding a cashless request or settling a claim. Timeline rules compare each claim's turnaround time with the limit that applies.
The service standards a provider has agreed to in its contract, such as claim processing time or call answer rate. Performance against each one is tracked and breaches are flagged.
The number IRDAI assigns to each approved insurance product. It ties a policy to the exact product wording that was filed.
The checks that confirm a customer's identity before a policy is issued or a claim is paid. They help prevent fraud and money laundering.
The rules and controls that stop insurance being used to disguise the proceeds of crime. They include customer checks, monitoring and reporting of suspicious transactions.
India's shared digital gateway for exchanging health claims between hospitals, insurers and TPAs. It uses the FHIR data standard.
A claim where the insurer pays the hospital directly, so the patient does not pay first. The hospital asks for approval before or during treatment.
A claim where the policyholder pays the hospital and is repaid by the insurer afterwards. It is assessed from the bills and medical records submitted.
The insurer's approval, given before or during a hospital stay, to cover treatment on a cashless basis. Regulations set how quickly the request must be decided.
A formal decision to reject a claim in full. The reason must be stated, recorded and communicated to the customer.
The process of approving a hospital to join the insurer's network for cashless treatment. It covers due diligence, agreed tariffs and periodic review.
A complaint from a customer about a policy, a claim or service. Regulations set timelines for acknowledging and resolving it, with escalation to the Ombudsman.
Deciding whether to insure someone, on what terms and at what price. Exceptions to the underwriting rules need a recorded approval.
IRDAI's online portal where policyholders register and track complaints against insurers. Complaints raised there are logged as grievances.

The combined practice of directing an organisation, managing what could go wrong, and proving that laws and rules are followed. This platform keeps all three in one place so they can be traced to each other.
The action taken to fix a problem that was found, and to stop it happening again. Each one is tracked to completion and then verified as effective by someone independent.
A measure of how well something is working, such as the share of claims settled within the timeline. Each one here shows its calculation rule.
An early-warning measure showing that a risk is becoming more likely, such as rising claim rejections. It turns amber or red when it crosses the thresholds you set.
A traffic-light status. Red needs action now, amber needs attention, and green is within limits.
Splitting a task so that no single person can both carry it out and approve it. For example, the person who raises a corrective action cannot verify it.
The senior person accountable for the organisation meeting its legal and regulatory duties. In this platform the role approves obligations and compliance conclusions.
The senior person accountable for identifying and managing the organisation's risks. In this platform the role approves risk assessments and risk acceptance.
The senior person accountable for protecting systems and data. Information security registers and incidents are overseen by this role.
A named set of rules or standards the organisation follows, such as an IRDAI regulation or ISO 27001. Obligations and control mappings are grouped under it.
One numbered provision inside a regulation or standard. Obligations point back to the exact clause they come from.
One specific thing the organisation must do or not do because a law, regulation or contract says so. It counts towards compliance figures only after a compliance officer approves it.
Whether an obligation applies to this organisation, given its licences, products and activities. Obligations marked not applicable are excluded from the figures, with the reason recorded.
A safeguard that reduces a risk or helps meet an obligation, such as a second approval or an access review. Controls are tested to show that they work.
A document or data set that proves a control was carried out. It is reviewed by a person before it is accepted, and it expires.
A confirmed weakness or breach identified by an audit, a test or a check. It stays open until corrective action is completed and closure is approved.
The size of a risk before any controls are considered. It is scored as likelihood multiplied by impact, out of 25.
The risk that remains after the controls in place are taken into account. This is the figure compared with the risk appetite.
The amount of risk the organisation is willing to accept. A residual risk above this level needs treatment or a formally approved acceptance.
A grid that plots risks by likelihood and impact. Risks in the darker cells towards the top right need attention first.
Being able to follow one requirement from the regulation through to the control, evidence, test, finding and fix. It is what an auditor or regulator asks to see.
An auditor's record of the procedure performed, what was examined and the result. Workpapers support the conclusions in the audit report.
Matching two sets of records, such as claims paid against bank payments, to find and explain differences. Unexplained differences are followed up.
Testing a selected portion of records instead of every one, and drawing a conclusion about the whole. The selection method and seed are recorded so the sample can be reproduced.
India's law on how organisations collect, use and protect personal data. It requires notice, consent or another lawful basis, security safeguards and breach reporting.
Information that can identify a person, such as a name, phone number or policy number. Fields holding it are marked, masked in exports and never sent to an AI model by default.
Signing in with two proofs of identity: a password and a code from an authenticator app on your phone. A stolen password alone is then not enough to get in.
Signing in through your organisation's own identity system, such as Microsoft Entra ID, Google or Okta. People use one account, and access ends when that account is disabled.
The open standard this platform uses for single sign-on. It lets your identity provider confirm who a person is without sharing their password.
The six-digit code an authenticator app shows, which changes every 30 seconds. It is the second step when multi-factor authentication is on.
The national agency for cyber security incidents. Certain incidents must be reported to it within a fixed number of hours.
The plan for keeping essential services running during a disruption. It is tested periodically and the results are recorded.
Restoring systems and data after a serious failure. Tests measure how quickly service returns and how much data could be lost.
The longest time a system may be unavailable after a failure. A disaster recovery test checks whether this target was met.
The greatest amount of recent data, measured in time, that may be lost in a failure. It determines how often backups must run.

glossary.full: International standard for information security management
glossary.text: A widely used standard describing how to manage information security systematically. Controls here can be mapped to its requirements.
An independent audit report on a service provider's security, availability and confidentiality controls. Insurers often ask vendors for one.

glossary.full: National Institute of Standards and Technology Cybersecurity Framework
glossary.text: A voluntary framework that organises cyber security work into govern, identify, protect, detect, respond and recover. It is offered here as an optional mapping.
The encrypted way a browser talks to a website. It stops others on the network reading or altering what is sent.
Software that drafts, summarises or flags items for a person to review. Here it only recommends: approvals and compliance conclusions are always made by people.
A defined way for one computer system to send data to or request data from another. Other systems feed claims and evidence into this platform through it.
Reading the text out of a scanned page or image so it can be searched and analysed. It is used for circulars that arrive as scanned documents.
An international standard format for exchanging healthcare data, including claims. India's National Health Claims Exchange uses it.
A simple spreadsheet file format that almost every system can read and write. Registers can be imported from and exported to it.
A message one system sends to another the moment something happens. Workflows can be started by one, or can send one to tools such as Slack or Teams.
A sequence of automatic steps, such as creating a task, asking for approval and sending a reminder, started by an event. People still make the decisions inside it.
A small read-only program that gathers proof from another system, such as who has administrator access. It sends the result here as evidence for a control.
An automation tool that connects systems through visual workflows. Ready-made n8n workflows are supplied for collecting evidence and sending alerts.
The system that holds employee records. It can supply joiner and leaver data for access reviews and training.
A system that collects security logs and raises alerts on suspicious activity. Its alerts can be fed in as security incidents.
The tool used to log and track IT requests, incidents and changes, such as Jira or ServiceNow. Tickets can be collected as evidence of a control operating.
The system that records customer contacts and service requests. Grievances can be fed from it.
The finance and operations system of record. It can supply data for financial reconciliations.

agents.name: Regulatory Intelligence Agent
agents.does: Reads a regulatory document and proposes clauses and obligations for the compliance team to validate.

agents.name: Compliance Mapping Agent
agents.does: Recommends which existing controls address an obligation, or drafts a new control where there is a gap.

agents.name: Risk Assessment Agent
agents.does: Suggests likelihood, impact and control effectiveness from linked controls, tests, findings and KRIs.

agents.name: Evidence Validation Agent
agents.does: Checks evidence for completeness, relevance, validity dates and inconsistencies before a reviewer decides.

agents.name: Claims Audit Agent
agents.does: Looks across claims and exceptions for unusual patterns by TPA, hospital, override and rejection reason.

agents.name: Third-Party Risk Agent
agents.does: Summarises a TPA, hospital or vendor's weak areas from assessments, SLAs and incidents, with follow-up actions.

agents.name: Audit Reporting Agent
agents.does: Drafts the audit report from recorded findings, and suggests root cause lines of enquiry for a finding.

items.report:
DRAFT AUDIT REPORT: Claims operations audit 2026 (AUD-0001)

1. Scope and objectives
Cashless and reimbursement claims processed in the last two quarters.
Assess turnaround compliance, rejection controls and approval authority.

2. Work performed
4 of 4 planned procedures completed. 2 resulted in observations.

3. Summary of findings
2 high, 1 medium, 1 low

4. Detailed findings
4.1 Approval authority overridden without recorded justification [High] (FND-0009) [S3]
   Observation: Three approvals above L1 limit by L1 users.
   Root cause: Authority matrix not enforced for manual override path.
   Status: CAPA in progress

4.2 Cashless pre-authorisation decisions exceeded one hour in 13% of sampled cases [High] (FND-0007) [S5]
   Observation: Sample of 60 requests; 8 exceeded the limit without a documented reason.
   Root cause: Single-shift staffing at the hub; no automated queue alert.
   Status: CAPA in progress

4.3 Rejection letters did not cite the policy clause in 5 of 30 samples [Medium] (FND-0008) [S4]
   Observation: Reason given in general terms only.
   Root cause: Template allows free text without a clause field.
   Status: Pending verification

4.4 Discharge authorisation escalation log incomplete [Low] (FND-0012) [S2]
   Observation: Escalations not logged for weekend shifts.
   Root cause: Weekend roster missed in procedure.
   Status: Closed

5. Management actions
Corrective and preventive actions are tracked in the CAPA register against each finding.

This draft was generated for auditor review. It contains no audit opinion; conclusions are the auditor's.

glossary.text: A licensed company that processes health insurance claims on the insurer's behalf, including cashless approvals at hospitals. The insurer remains accountable for what the TPA does, so its performance and controls are overseen here.

glossary.full: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
glossary.text: The regulator that licenses and supervises insurers, TPAs and intermediaries in India. Most obligations in the regulatory library come from its regulations and circulars.
The time taken to finish a step, such as deciding a cashless request or settling a claim. Timeline rules compare each claim's turnaround time with the limit that applies.
The service standards a provider has agreed to in its contract, such as claim processing time or call answer rate. Performance against each one is tracked and breaches are flagged.
The number IRDAI assigns to each approved insurance product. It ties a policy to the exact product wording that was filed.
The checks that confirm a customer's identity before a policy is issued or a claim is paid. They help prevent fraud and money laundering.
The rules and controls that stop insurance being used to disguise the proceeds of crime. They include customer checks, monitoring and reporting of suspicious transactions.
India's shared digital gateway for exchanging health claims between hospitals, insurers and TPAs. It uses the FHIR data standard.
A claim where the insurer pays the hospital directly, so the patient does not pay first. The hospital asks for approval before or during treatment.
A claim where the policyholder pays the hospital and is repaid by the insurer afterwards. It is assessed from the bills and medical records submitted.
The insurer's approval, given before or during a hospital stay, to cover treatment on a cashless basis. Regulations set how quickly the request must be decided.
A formal decision to reject a claim in full. The reason must be stated, recorded and communicated to the customer.
The process of approving a hospital to join the insurer's network for cashless treatment. It covers due diligence, agreed tariffs and periodic review.
A complaint from a customer about a policy, a claim or service. Regulations set timelines for acknowledging and resolving it, with escalation to the Ombudsman.
Deciding whether to insure someone, on what terms and at what price. Exceptions to the underwriting rules need a recorded approval.
IRDAI's online portal where policyholders register and track complaints against insurers. Complaints raised there are logged as grievances.

The combined practice of directing an organisation, managing what could go wrong, and proving that laws and rules are followed. This platform keeps all three in one place so they can be traced to each other.
The action taken to fix a problem that was found, and to stop it happening again. Each one is tracked to completion and then verified as effective by someone independent.
A measure of how well something is working, such as the share of claims settled within the timeline. Each one here shows its calculation rule.
An early-warning measure showing that a risk is becoming more likely, such as rising claim rejections. It turns amber or red when it crosses the thresholds you set.
A traffic-light status. Red needs action now, amber needs attention, and green is within limits.
Splitting a task so that no single person can both carry it out and approve it. For example, the person who raises a corrective action cannot verify it.
The senior person accountable for the organisation meeting its legal and regulatory duties. In this platform the role approves obligations and compliance conclusions.
The senior person accountable for identifying and managing the organisation's risks. In this platform the role approves risk assessments and risk acceptance.
The senior person accountable for protecting systems and data. Information security registers and incidents are overseen by this role.
A named set of rules or standards the organisation follows, such as an IRDAI regulation or ISO 27001. Obligations and control mappings are grouped under it.
One numbered provision inside a regulation or standard. Obligations point back to the exact clause they come from.
One specific thing the organisation must do or not do because a law, regulation or contract says so. It counts towards compliance figures only after a compliance officer approves it.
Whether an obligation applies to this organisation, given its licences, products and activities. Obligations marked not applicable are excluded from the figures, with the reason recorded.
A safeguard that reduces a risk or helps meet an obligation, such as a second approval or an access review. Controls are tested to show that they work.
A document or data set that proves a control was carried out. It is reviewed by a person before it is accepted, and it expires.
A confirmed weakness or breach identified by an audit, a test or a check. It stays open until corrective action is completed and closure is approved.
The size of a risk before any controls are considered. It is scored as likelihood multiplied by impact, out of 25.
The risk that remains after the controls in place are taken into account. This is the figure compared with the risk appetite.
The amount of risk the organisation is willing to accept. A residual risk above this level needs treatment or a formally approved acceptance.
A grid that plots risks by likelihood and impact. Risks in the darker cells towards the top right need attention first.
Being able to follow one requirement from the regulation through to the control, evidence, test, finding and fix. It is what an auditor or regulator asks to see.
An auditor's record of the procedure performed, what was examined and the result. Workpapers support the conclusions in the audit report.
Matching two sets of records, such as claims paid against bank payments, to find and explain differences. Unexplained differences are followed up.
Testing a selected portion of records instead of every one, and drawing a conclusion about the whole. The selection method and seed are recorded so the sample can be reproduced.
India's law on how organisations collect, use and protect personal data. It requires notice, consent or another lawful basis, security safeguards and breach reporting.
Information that can identify a person, such as a name, phone number or policy number. Fields holding it are marked, masked in exports and never sent to an AI model by default.
Signing in with two proofs of identity: a password and a code from an authenticator app on your phone. A stolen password alone is then not enough to get in.
Signing in through your organisation's own identity system, such as Microsoft Entra ID, Google or Okta. People use one account, and access ends when that account is disabled.
The open standard this platform uses for single sign-on. It lets your identity provider confirm who a person is without sharing their password.
The six-digit code an authenticator app shows, which changes every 30 seconds. It is the second step when multi-factor authentication is on.
The national agency for cyber security incidents. Certain incidents must be reported to it within a fixed number of hours.
The plan for keeping essential services running during a disruption. It is tested periodically and the results are recorded.
Restoring systems and data after a serious failure. Tests measure how quickly service returns and how much data could be lost.
The longest time a system may be unavailable after a failure. A disaster recovery test checks whether this target was met.
The greatest amount of recent data, measured in time, that may be lost in a failure. It determines how often backups must run.

glossary.full: International standard for information security management
glossary.text: A widely used standard describing how to manage information security systematically. Controls here can be mapped to its requirements.
An independent audit report on a service provider's security, availability and confidentiality controls. Insurers often ask vendors for one.

glossary.full: National Institute of Standards and Technology Cybersecurity Framework
glossary.text: A voluntary framework that organises cyber security work into govern, identify, protect, detect, respond and recover. It is offered here as an optional mapping.
The encrypted way a browser talks to a website. It stops others on the network reading or altering what is sent.
Software that drafts, summarises or flags items for a person to review. Here it only recommends: approvals and compliance conclusions are always made by people.
A defined way for one computer system to send data to or request data from another. Other systems feed claims and evidence into this platform through it.
Reading the text out of a scanned page or image so it can be searched and analysed. It is used for circulars that arrive as scanned documents.
An international standard format for exchanging healthcare data, including claims. India's National Health Claims Exchange uses it.
A simple spreadsheet file format that almost every system can read and write. Registers can be imported from and exported to it.
A message one system sends to another the moment something happens. Workflows can be started by one, or can send one to tools such as Slack or Teams.
A sequence of automatic steps, such as creating a task, asking for approval and sending a reminder, started by an event. People still make the decisions inside it.
A small read-only program that gathers proof from another system, such as who has administrator access. It sends the result here as evidence for a control.
An automation tool that connects systems through visual workflows. Ready-made n8n workflows are supplied for collecting evidence and sending alerts.
The system that holds employee records. It can supply joiner and leaver data for access reviews and training.
A system that collects security logs and raises alerts on suspicious activity. Its alerts can be fed in as security incidents.
The tool used to log and track IT requests, incidents and changes, such as Jira or ServiceNow. Tickets can be collected as evidence of a control operating.
The system that records customer contacts and service requests. Grievances can be fed from it.
The finance and operations system of record. It can supply data for financial reconciliations.

kpis.name: Regulatory obligation coverage
kpis.rule: Approved, applicable obligations that have a department and an owner, divided by all approved, applicable obligations.

kpis.name: Control coverage
kpis.rule: Approved, applicable obligations with at least one mapped control, divided by all approved, applicable obligations.

kpis.name: Evidence completeness
kpis.rule: Active controls with at least one accepted, unexpired evidence record, divided by all active controls.

kpis.name: Control test pass rate
kpis.rule: Active controls whose latest test passed (with or without exceptions), divided by active controls that have been tested. Untested controls are excluded.

kpis.name: Audit closure on time
kpis.rule: Findings closed on or before their due date, divided by findings that are closed or past due. Open findings not yet due are excluded.

kpis.name: Claims within timelines
kpis.rule: Evaluated claims with no open or confirmed exception (documented extensions count as within), divided by evaluated claims. Claims still inside their limits are excluded.

kpis.name: TPA assessments in date
kpis.rule: Active TPAs with an assessment that is not past its reassessment date, divided by active TPAs.

kpis.name: CAPA effectiveness
kpis.rule: Corrective actions verified as effective, divided by actions whose effectiveness has been assessed.

kpis.name: Mandatory training completion
kpis.rule: Mandatory training assignments completed, divided by those completed or past their due date. Assignments not yet due are excluded.

kpis.name: Risk reduction
kpis.rule: Total inherent score minus total residual score, divided by total inherent score, across open risks that have been scored.
